titulo: Pretérito perfecto: saying what you did today: Haber + participle

aula.titulo: Pretérito perfecto: saying what you did today
aula.objetivo: Form the pretérito perfecto with haber + past participle (regular and irregular), use it with hoy, esta mañana, esta semana, ya, todavía no, alguna vez and nunca, and see where it overlaps with — and differs from — the English present perfect.

itens.pt: ever, at some point (in one's life)

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: the «pretérito perfecto» talks about something that has already happened within a period that hasn't ended yet: today, this week, this month, this year; or something that still matters right now: «Ya he comido» (I've already eaten). STEP 2: build it in two parts: «haber» in the present + the past participle. The forms of «haber» are: he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han. STEP 3: the past participle of -ar verbs ends in «-ado»: hablar → hablado, trabajar → trabajado. -er and -ir verbs end in «-ido»: comer → comido, vivir → vivido. STEP 4: the participle never changes — it has no gender and no number. You say «Ella ha comido» and «Ellas han comido»; only «haber» changes. STEP 5: nothing ever comes between «haber» and the participle. Negation and pronouns go before «haber»: «No he comido», «Me he levantado», «Ya me he duchado». The adverb «ya» goes either before «he» or after the participle: «Ya he comido» or «He comido ya», never «He ya comido». STEP 6: the most common markers are: «hoy, esta mañana, esta tarde, esta semana, este mes, este año, ya, todavía no, alguna vez, nunca, siempre». STEP 7: the most important thing to watch: English «I have eaten» can mean either a completed action in an unfinished period (which matches Spanish «he comido» closely) or an ongoing habit, and it never changes form for that difference — Spanish «he comido» is always the first kind, a single completed action: it means «I ate (today)» or «I've already eaten», never a recurring habit. Never use «tener» in place of «haber» to build this tense: «tengo comido» is not the pretérito perfecto. STEP 8: in Spain the pretérito perfecto is used for what happened today; in much of Latin America, the pretérito indefinido (which you'll see at A2) is preferred even for today: «Hoy comí».
blocos.comparacao: English «I have eaten» and Spanish «he comido» line up closely for a single completed action within a period that hasn't ended («I've eaten already» ↔ «ya he comido»), so that part transfers well. Where it gets tricky is that English «I have eaten» can also describe a repeated habit over time («I have eaten here for years»), a sense the Spanish pretérito perfecto never carries — Spanish always treats «he comido» as one finished event, equivalent to «I ate» or «I've already eaten», and nothing more.

exemplos.ru: Esta semana hemos estudiado cinco horas.
exemplos.pt: This week we studied for five hours.

exemplos.ru: Todavía no he hablado con Ana.
exemplos.pt: I haven't talked to Ana yet.

erros.motivo: The auxiliary is «haber»; «tener» doesn't form this compound tense.
The auxiliary agrees with the subject: «ella ha».
Nothing comes between «haber» and the participle.

blocos.enunciado: Say out loud what you've done today so far, in five sentences: «Hoy me he levantado… He desayunado… He trabajado…» Finish with what you haven't done yet: «Todavía no he…»
Say five sentences about your likes with «me gusta» and «me gustan». Then ask a friend if they like the same things, with «¿Y a ti?».
